title: Alice and Books for Children
objective: After this level you can explain how Lewis Carroll's Alice broke with children's books that preached.
summary: Lewis Carroll's Alice (1865) appeared when children's books taught morals. It parodied moral verses and made a silly Duchess the one hunting for morals.

cards.headline: Alice's first complaint is about a boring book.
cards.body: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland opens with Alice peeping into her sister's book: "and what is the use of a book," thought Alice "without pictures or conversations?" When it appeared in 1865, children's books were generally meant to teach moral lessons. Alice was about to break the rules.

cards.headline: A story told in a rowing boat
cards.body: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, a lecturer in mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford. On July 4, 1862, he rowed the three Liddell children up the Thames and told them a tale about a girl named Alice. Alice Liddell asked him to write it down. It grew into Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, published in 1865 with pictures by John Tenniel.

cards.headline: A busy bee turns into a grinning crocodile

items.label: Lewis Carroll, 1865
points: He welcomes fish "With gently smiling jaws"

cards.headline: Everything's got a moral
cards.body: Carroll even puts a moral-hunter in the book. The Duchess tells Alice, "Everything's got a moral, if only you can find it," and pins one on remark after remark. Alice thinks, "How fond she is of finding morals in things!" The lesson-giver has become the joke. Critics were baffled at first, but by the end of the 19th century Alice was the most popular children's book in England.

questions.prompt: A new children's book ends every chapter with "And so, children, always tidy your room." Which tradition does it follow?

options.rationale: The Duchess finds morals everywhere, and that's the joke.

questions.explanation: Books that preach a lesson in every chapter are the kind Alice broke with, when children's books were generally meant to teach moral lessons.

questions.prompt: Fables usually state their moral at the end. What does Carroll's Duchess do with morals?

options.label: Refuses to give any moral at all
Finds one in everything, until morals sound silly
Tells Alice the fable of the fox and grapes
Hides every moral in a secret code for Alice to crack
options.rationale: She says them out loud, constantly.

questions.explanation: The Duchess insists "Everything's got a moral" and pins one on remark after remark, so the fable's lesson becomes a joke.
